---
name: pricing-packaging-tracker
argument-hint: "[competitor set, and prior capture if one exists]"
description: "Track competitor pricing and packaging as a diffable time series. Use when monitoring tiers, gates, limits, and price moves on a monthly or quarterly cadence."
intent: >-
  Capture competitor public pricing pages into a stable schema, diff against the prior capture, and
  report tier changes, price moves, feature-gate shifts, and packaging restructures with URLs and
  dates — because packaging changes signal strategy earlier than price changes do.
type: workflow
theme: market-intelligence
best_for:
  - "Keeping battle-card pricing sections current without manual screenshot archaeology"
  - "Catching packaging restructures — the earliest public signal of a strategy shift"
  - "Building the pricing time series that grounds your own pricing decisions"
scenarios:
  - "Baseline the pricing pages of our four main competitors, then track monthly"
  - "Did anyone in our space change pricing or packaging this quarter?"
estimated_time: "15-30 min per run"
---

# Pricing & Packaging Tracker

## Purpose

Track competitor pricing and packaging as a **diffable time series**, not a screenshot: **capture (or
diff) → structure changes → price changes → signals → next-step options.** The stable capture schema
is the point — run N diffs against run N-1, so the report is what *moved*, with evidence. And the
skill watches structure as closely as numbers, because packaging changes (gates, limits, tier
restructures) usually signal strategy earlier than price changes do: a tier that disappears telegraphs
a move upmarket months before the price list admits it.

## Input

**Works best with:** the competitor set to track (or the snapshot they came from), and the prior
pricing capture if one exists — that's what turns this run into a delta report.
**Also useful:** your own pricing context, if the comparison should include you.

Input supplied inline with the invocation — text after the skill name, a pasted context dump, or an
appended `ARGUMENTS:` line — counts as answers already given. Use it against the question budget;
don't re-ask.

**Arriving empty-handed? That works too.** With no prior capture the skill runs **baseline mode**:
full capture per competitor, and the delta value starts next run. With no competitor list, it asks —
that's one of its two budget questions.

**Example invocation:** `Pricing tracker on [Competitor A], [Competitor B], [Competitor C] — prior
capture from April pasted below.`

## Key Concepts

- **Governing protocol:** honors the [`autonomous-investigation`](../autonomous-investigation/SKILL.md)
  contract — question budget of 2, Fact/Inference/Assumption labels, Just Enough Mode, stable schema,
  4-option Final Step. Discipline: SIGINT (pricing pages, site diffs) with FININT corroboration — see
  [`intelligence-collection-disciplines`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/intelligence-collection-disciplines/SKILL.md).
- **Time series, not screenshot.** A single capture is trivia; the sequence is intelligence. The
  schema never drifts between runs, because diffability is the entire value.
- **Structure over numbers.** Record tiers, billing units, feature gates, usage limits, free-tier
  boundaries, and enterprise-floor signals — not just prices. The gate moves first; the price
  follows.
- **"Contact sales" is data, honestly labeled.** Where pricing is opaque, track what *is* public
  (editions, gates, published floors) and mark the rest. Infer only with labels; never invent
  prices, tiers, limits, discounts, or negotiated figures.
- **When NOT to use:** you need pricing *strategy* advice →
  [`finance-based-pricing-advisor`](../finance-based-pricing-advisor/SKILL.md) (this tracks the
  market; it doesn't set your price); pricing is fully opaque across the whole set → expect thin
  results, and consider [`voice-of-customer-miner`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/voice-of-customer-miner/SKILL.md) or win/loss
  evidence instead.

## Application

1. **Determine mode.** Prior capture provided → delta mode (report changes only). None → baseline
   mode (full capture, then stop).
2. **Credit inline context**, then ask only the unanswered questions (max 2):
   1. Which competitors' pricing should I track?
   2. Prior capture to diff against, or is this the baseline?
3. **Capture from live pricing pages** — plan-comparison pages, published rate cards, credible
   pricing-change coverage — with URL and as-of date per competitor.
4. **Emit the schema below exactly** — diffability is the point.

### Output schema (do not reorder)

~~~markdown
# Pricing Capture / Delta Report

## 1. Run Header
**Competitor set:** | **Prior capture date:** [or "baseline run"] | **This run date:**

## 2. Pricing Capture (per competitor)
### [Competitor] — [pricing page URL, as-of date]
- **Tiers:** [name: price / unit / billing terms, one bullet each]
- **Key gates:** [which capabilities gate which tier, 2-4 bullets]
- **Usage limits:** [the limits that matter, 1-2 bullets]
- **Free tier / trial:** [boundary, 1 bullet]
- **Enterprise signals:** [published floors, "contact sales" scope]

(Baseline mode: full capture per competitor. Delta mode: this section
only for competitors with changes.)

## 3. Changes Since Last Capture (Delta Mode)
### [Competitor] — [4 to 8 word change summary]
- **Then / Now:** [old -> new, labeled Fact]
- **Evidence:** [URL, date]
- **Reading:** [Inference — repositioning, monetization push, response to whom?]

If nothing changed: "No pricing or packaging changes this cycle."

## 4. Signals
- [Cross-competitor patterns: direction of the market's pricing, labeled]
- [Implications for your pricing or battle cards: 2-3 bullets]

### Assumptions to Validate
- [Assumption 1] / [Assumption 2] / [Assumption 3]
~~~

A copy/paste fill-in version of this schema, with quality checks, lives in [`template.md`](template.md).

### Final Step (offer exactly 4 options)

1. Update battle card pricing sections from these changes ([`battle-card-builder`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/battle-card-builder/SKILL.md))
2. Deep-dive one competitor's packaging logic
3. Compare your pricing against this capture
4. Set the cadence and watchlist for the next run

Accept `1`, `2`, `3`, `4`, `1 and 2`, `Verbose Mode`, or a custom path.

## Examples

**A delta entry reading structure, not just price (fictional):**

> ### [Competitor B] — API access moved from Pro to new Scale tier
> - **Then / Now:** API access included in Pro ($79/seat) → gated behind new "Scale" tier
>   ($149/seat, 10-seat minimum) — **Fact**
> - **Evidence:** [pricing page vs. archived capture, URL, dates]
> - **Reading:** the price didn't change; the *gate* did. Developer-led accounts are being pushed
>   into a sales conversation — **Inference**: monetization push on their fastest-growing usage
>   pattern, and a window for us with API-first buyers while their community absorbs it.

**The cross-competitor signal:** three of four tracked competitors added usage-based add-ons this
quarter while holding seat prices flat — **Inference:** the market is testing consumption pricing
without headline price increases. Your pricing debate is no longer hypothetical; the Signals section
names the evidence.

See [`examples/sample.md`](examples/sample.md) for a complete worked delta run (fictional
FSM-software market) where both material moves are structural — a new tier and a relocated gate —
and no headline price changed at all. [`examples/sample-industrial.md`](examples/sample-industrial.md)
shows the fully opaque case: zero published prices, and structure as the only public signal.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Screenshot thinking.** Capturing once and calling it competitive pricing intel. The value
  compounds only on a cadence — baseline, then diff, forever.
- **Number fixation.** Reporting only price changes while a tier quietly gained a 5-seat minimum.
  Structure is the leading indicator; watch the gates.
- **Inventing the opaque.** Filling "contact sales" cells with plausible figures. Publish the
  honest boundary and label any inference — a battle card built on invented enterprise pricing
  detonates in a live deal.
- **Schema improvisation.** Reordering or "improving" the capture format between runs breaks every
  future diff. The schema is a contract with your own future runs.
- **Tracking without a consumer.** If no battle card, pricing review, or watch report consumes the
  output, the cadence dies quietly. Wire the Final Step's first option into a real artifact.

## References

- [`autonomous-investigation`](../autonomous-investigation/SKILL.md) (Workflow) — the governing protocol

# Pricing & Packaging Tracker

## Purpose

Track competitor pricing and packaging as a **diffable time series**, not a screenshot: **capture (or
diff) → structure changes → price changes → signals → next-step options.** The stable capture schema
is the point — run N diffs against run N-1, so the report is what *moved*, with evidence. And the
skill watches structure as closely as numbers, because packaging changes (gates, limits, tier
restructures) usually signal strategy earlier than price changes do: a tier that disappears telegraphs
a move upmarket months before the price list admits it.

## Input

**Works best with:** the competitor set to track (or the snapshot they came from), and the prior
pricing capture if one exists — that's what turns this run into a delta report.
**Also useful:** your own pricing context, if the comparison should include you.

Input supplied inline with the invocation — text after the skill name, a pasted context dump, or an
appended `ARGUMENTS:` line — counts as answers already given. Use it against the question budget;
don't re-ask.

**Arriving empty-handed? That works too.** With no prior capture the skill runs **baseline mode**:
full capture per competitor, and the delta value starts next run. With no competitor list, it asks —
that's one of its two budget questions.

**Example invocation:** `Pricing tracker on [Competitor A], [Competitor B], [Competitor C] — prior
capture from April pasted below.`

## Key Concepts

- **Governing protocol:** honors the [`autonomous-investigation`](../autonomous-investigation/SKILL.md)
  contract — question budget of 2, Fact/Inference/Assumption labels, Just Enough Mode, stable schema,
  4-option Final Step. Discipline: SIGINT (pricing pages, site diffs) with FININT corroboration — see
  [`intelligence-collection-disciplines`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/intelligence-collection-disciplines/SKILL.md).
- **Time series, not screenshot.** A single capture is trivia; the sequence is intelligence. The
  schema never drifts between runs, because diffability is the entire value.
- **Structure over numbers.** Record tiers, billing units, feature gates, usage limits, free-tier
  boundaries, and enterprise-floor signals — not just prices. The gate moves first; the price
  follows.
- **"Contact sales" is data, honestly labeled.** Where pricing is opaque, track what *is* public
  (editions, gates, published floors) and mark the rest. Infer only with labels; never invent
  prices, tiers, limits, discounts, or negotiated figures.
- **When NOT to use:** you need pricing *strategy* advice →
  [`finance-based-pricing-advisor`](../finance-based-pricing-advisor/SKILL.md) (this tracks the
  market; it doesn't set your price); pricing is fully opaque across the whole set → expect thin
  results, and consider [`voice-of-customer-miner`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/voice-of-customer-miner/SKILL.md) or win/loss
  evidence instead.

## Application

1. **Determine mode.** Prior capture provided → delta mode (report changes only). None → baseline
   mode (full capture, then stop).
2. **Credit inline context**, then ask only the unanswered questions (max 2):
   1. Which competitors' pricing should I track?
   2. Prior capture to diff against, or is this the baseline?
3. **Capture from live pricing pages** — plan-comparison pages, published rate cards, credible
   pricing-change coverage — with URL and as-of date per competitor.
4. **Emit the schema below exactly** — diffability is the point.

### Output schema (do not reorder)

~~~markdown
# Pricing Capture / Delta Report

## 1. Run Header
**Competitor set:** | **Prior capture date:** [or "baseline run"] | **This run date:**

## 2. Pricing Capture (per competitor)
### [Competitor] — [pricing page URL, as-of date]
- **Tiers:** [name: price / unit / billing terms, one bullet each]
- **Key gates:** [which capabilities gate which tier, 2-4 bullets]
- **Usage limits:** [the limits that matter, 1-2 bullets]
- **Free tier / trial:** [boundary, 1 bullet]
- **Enterprise signals:** [published floors, "contact sales" scope]

(Baseline mode: full capture per competitor. Delta mode: this section
only for competitors with changes.)

## 3. Changes Since Last Capture (Delta Mode)
### [Competitor] — [4 to 8 word change summary]
- **Then / Now:** [old -> new, labeled Fact]
- **Evidence:** [URL, date]
- **Reading:** [Inference — repositioning, monetization push, response to whom?]

If nothing changed: "No pricing or packaging changes this cycle."

## 4. Signals
- [Cross-competitor patterns: direction of the market's pricing, labeled]
- [Implications for your pricing or battle cards: 2-3 bullets]

### Assumptions to Validate
- [Assumption 1] / [Assumption 2] / [Assumption 3]
~~~

A copy/paste fill-in version of this schema, with quality checks, lives in [`template.md`](template.md).

### Final Step (offer exactly 4 options)

1. Update battle card pricing sections from these changes ([`battle-card-builder`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/battle-card-builder/SKILL.md))
2. Deep-dive one competitor's packaging logic
3. Compare your pricing against this capture
4. Set the cadence and watchlist for the next run

Accept `1`, `2`, `3`, `4`, `1 and 2`, `Verbose Mode`, or a custom path.

## Examples

**A delta entry reading structure, not just price (fictional):**

> ### [Competitor B] — API access moved from Pro to new Scale tier
> - **Then / Now:** API access included in Pro ($79/seat) → gated behind new "Scale" tier
>   ($149/seat, 10-seat minimum) — **Fact**
> - **Evidence:** [pricing page vs. archived capture, URL, dates]
> - **Reading:** the price didn't change; the *gate* did. Developer-led accounts are being pushed
>   into a sales conversation — **Inference**: monetization push on their fastest-growing usage
>   pattern, and a window for us with API-first buyers while their community absorbs it.

**The cross-competitor signal:** three of four tracked competitors added usage-based add-ons this
quarter while holding seat prices flat — **Inference:** the market is testing consumption pricing
without headline price increases. Your pricing debate is no longer hypothetical; the Signals section
names the evidence.

See [`examples/sample.md`](examples/sample.md) for a complete worked delta run (fictional
FSM-software market) where both material moves are structural — a new tier and a relocated gate —
and no headline price changed at all. [`examples/sample-industrial.md`](examples/sample-industrial.md)
shows the fully opaque case: zero published prices, and structure as the only public signal.

## Common Pitfalls

- **Screenshot thinking.** Capturing once and calling it competitive pricing intel. The value
  compounds only on a cadence — baseline, then diff, forever.
- **Number fixation.** Reporting only price changes while a tier quietly gained a 5-seat minimum.
  Structure is the leading indicator; watch the gates.
- **Inventing the opaque.** Filling "contact sales" cells with plausible figures. Publish the
  honest boundary and label any inference — a battle card built on invented enterprise pricing
  detonates in a live deal.
- **Schema improvisation.** Reordering or "improving" the capture format between runs breaks every
  future diff. The schema is a contract with your own future runs.
- **Tracking without a consumer.** If no battle card, pricing review, or watch report consumes the
  output, the cadence dies quietly. Wire the Final Step's first option into a real artifact.

## References

- [`autonomous-investigation`](../autonomous-investigation/SKILL.md) (Workflow) — the governing protocol
- [`intelligence-collection-disciplines`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/intelligence-collection-disciplines/SKILL.md) (Component) — SIGINT sources: Wayback diffs, pricing-page monitoring
- [`competitive-intel-watch`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/competitive-intel-watch/SKILL.md) (Workflow) — the broader watch this tracker feeds
- [`battle-card-builder`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/battle-card-builder/SKILL.md) (Workflow) — consumes the pricing snapshot sections
- [`finance-based-pricing-advisor`](../finance-based-pricing-advisor/SKILL.md) (Interactive) — sets *your* price; this skill informs it with market evidence
- Adapted from `market-intelligence/pricing-packaging-tracker-prompt.md` in the
  `https://github.com/deanpeters/product-manager-prompts` repo.

intent: >-

  plays available at the decline inflection — extend the product, replace it with a successor, or
  retire it. Includes the mature-to-declining transition questions, the seven replacement hazards
  with a risk register, and a portfolio worksheet for deciding across a product line.
type: component
theme: product-lifecycle
best_for:
  - "Deciding whether a fading product should be extended, replaced, or retired"
  - "Diagnosing whether a product has actually crossed from mature into decline"
  - "Running the play decision across a whole product line, not one product at a time"
scenarios:
  - "Revenue is flattening on our flagship and people are arguing about a rewrite versus a refresh"
  - "We have four aging SKUs and no consistent way to decide what happens to each"

# Product Lifecycle Plays

## Purpose

Decide what to do with a product that has stopped growing. There are three plays — **extend**,
**replace**, **retire** — and picking the wrong one is expensive in a different way each time. This
skill gives you the stage diagnosis, the criteria that discriminate the plays, and the hazard
register for the one that goes wrong most often.

Most teams skip straight to a play. Someone says "let's rebuild it" or "let's kill it," and the
argument that follows is about the answer rather than the diagnosis. The diagnosis is the work.

## Input

**Works best with:** The product or product line, and the signal that prompted the question —
flattening revenue, rising support costs, a competitor move, a strategy shift.

**Also useful:** Revenue and margin trend, customer counts and concentration, support load, what
else in the portfolio is adjacent, and how much investment appetite exists.

Anything supplied with the invocation itself — text after the skill name, a pasted context dump, or
an appended `ARGUMENTS:` line — counts as answers already given. Use it and skip whatever it
covers; don't re-ask.

**Arriving empty-handed? That works too.** Bring the product name and a hunch. The stage diagnosis
runs off the transition questions below, which are answerable from what a PM already knows without
pulling a report.

**Example invocations:**
- `Revenue on our reporting module has been flat for six quarters — extend, replace, or retire?`
- `Run the play worksheet across our four aging SKUs.`

---

## Key Concepts

### The Product Life Cycle

Five stages, each with a different economic job:

| Stage | What's happening | The job |
|---|---|---|
| **Design** | Concept, prototype, launch planning | Prove the problem is real |
| **Introduce** | Launch, awareness, first sales | Find the early adopters |
| **Grow** | Rapid sales, market expansion | Build the customer base |
| **Mature** | Peak sales, peak profitability | Defend position, maximize margin |
| **Decline** | Falling sales, phase-out planning | Maximize remaining value |

**Go-to-market happens at the front. End-of-life happens at the back. The plays live at the
mature-to-decline inflection** — which is exactly where most teams have no framework and default to
whoever argues hardest.

### The Strategy Grid

What "good" looks like changes by stage. Each lever tells you something different about where you
actually are:

| Lever | Mature | Declining |
|---|---|---|
| Marketing objective | Defend market position | Maximize remaining value |
| Competition | Emphasize brand loyalty | Consolidate customer base |
| Product | Optimize | Extended CX, streamline support |
| Promotion | Loyalty incentives | Migration campaigns |
| Place (distribution) | Optimize channels | Focus on profitable channels |
| Price | Value-add bundles | Selective discounting |
| Data strategy | Predictive modeling | Transition planning data |

### The Transition Questions

**This is the diagnostic.** For each lever, ask the question that tells you whether you've crossed
from mature into decline. Answering "yes" to four or more means you are in decline regardless of
what the revenue chart says this quarter:

| Lever | Ask |
|---|---|
| Marketing objective | Is defending market share still profitable? |
| Competition | Are loyalty efforts no longer retaining users? |
| Product | Are legacy support costs becoming unsustainable? |
| Promotion | Should we be running migration campaigns instead of loyalty ones? |
| Place | Are we losing money on certain distribution channels? |
| Price | Are our value-add bundles losing effectiveness? |
| Data strategy | Is our data shifting from predictive to transitional? |

**Why ask rather than measure:** revenue lags. A product can post a flat quarter while every one of
these has already turned. The questions catch the inflection before the chart does.

### The Three Plays

**Extension Play** — introduce a new variant or additional features to an existing product line.

*Reasons why:* expand into new customer segments · meet diverse customer needs · differentiate from
competitors · boost sales with new variants · strengthen brand loyalty.

*Shape:* the existing product keeps running; you add alongside. Cheapest play, lowest risk, and the
one most often dismissed because it isn't exciting.

**Replacement Play** — introduce a new product to take the place of an existing one, offering
similar or improved capability while phasing the old one out.

*Reasons why:* address supply issues · reduce production costs · eliminate obsolete or unused
features · align with strategic goals · comply with regulatory change.

*Shape:* **GTM and EOL happen simultaneously.** This is the expensive play, and the reason is
structural — see below.

**Retirement Play** — phase the product out without a successor of your own.

*Reasons why:* costs exceed revenue · strategic exit from the market · the core problem stopped
existing · technology made it obsolete.

*Shape:* pure EOL. Customers land somewhere else, possibly a competitor, and the goal becomes
losing the product without losing the customer.

### Why Replacement Is the Expensive Play

On a replacement you are running a **launch and a retirement at the same time, for two products
that compete with each other.** Every GTM risk and every EOL risk applies at once, plus one that
only exists here: cannibalization between your own two products.

Both directions of that failure are instructive:
- **Kodak** feared cannibalizing film and starved its digital business. The fear cost the market.
- **Amgen** cannibalized Epogen with Aranesp deliberately. It worked, and still produced complex
  pricing dynamics they had to manage for years.

Fear it and you lose the future; ignore it and you lose margin. Plan for it and you get a
transition.

### The Seven Replacement Hazards

What goes wrong on a replacement play, with the pattern each one leaves:

| # | Hazard | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **GTM process failure** | The successor exists but nobody adopts it (Zune) |
| 2 | **Delayed market entry** | Late launch lets competitors define the category (BlackBerry) |
| 3 | **Internal misalignment** | Siloed R&D, marketing, and sales blunt the launch (New Coke) |
| 4 | **External forces** | Backlash, safety, or macro shocks force withdrawal (Google Glass) |
| 5 | **Regulatory risk** | Compliance missed, or the successor triggers new obligations |
| 6 | **Unexpected cannibalization** | The two products fight each other (Kodak, Amgen) |
| 7 | **Poor EOL management** | The successor lands but the old product's exit is botched (Vista, AT&T POTS, Nest Revolv) |

**Hazard 7 is the one this repo's EOL suite exists to prevent** — and it's the one teams discount
most, because by the time they're planning the launch, the retirement feels like paperwork.

### The Risk Register

For each hazard that applies, fill five columns. The fifth is the one people skip:

| Risk | Probability | Impact | Mitigation | Contingency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| What could adversely affect the business case? | How likely? | How bad? | How do we reduce the probability? | **What is Plan B?** |

A register with no contingency column is a worry list. Plan B is what makes it a plan.

### Anti-Patterns (what this is NOT)
- **Not a growth framework.** Where the next tranche of growth comes from is a different question —
  see `ansoff-matrix` and `organic-growth-advisor`.
- **Not a forecast.** It reasons about stage and direction, not numbers.
- **Not automatic.** Decline is not a death sentence; a mature product throwing off margin with low
  support cost is a harvest, not a project.
- **Not one product at a time, necessarily.** The worksheet runs across a line, and the plays
  interact — two products can't both be the replacement.

---

## Application

Use `template.md` for the worksheet and risk register.

### Step 1: Diagnose the stage

Run the seven transition questions. Count the yeses:

- **0-1 yes** — mature and healthy. The question isn't a play, it's whether to invest more
- **2-3 yes** — mature and softening. Extension play territory; watch quarterly
- **4-5 yes** — crossing into decline. Pick a play deliberately, now
- **6-7 yes** — in decline. Replace or retire; extension likely postpones a decision rather than
  changing an outcome

Write down which questions came back yes. The *pattern* discriminates the plays more than the count
does.

### Step 2: Identify what's driving the pressure

Three sources, and they point at different plays:

| Pressure | Signal | Points toward |
|---|---|---|
| **Demand-side** | Needs shifted, segments moved, competitors differentiated | **Extend** — if the core still solves a real problem for someone |
| **Supply/cost-side** | Components EOL, production cost, support load, strategy shift | **Replace** — the problem is your economics, not the customer's need |
| **Capability-side** | Technology obsolete, architecture at its limit, regulation changed | **Replace** or **Retire** — depends on whether the need survives the technology |

**The trap:** supply-side pressure feels like a customer problem when it reaches the roadmap. "We
need to rebuild this" often means "our costs are bad," which is a legitimate reason for a
replacement — but say it out loud, because it changes what success looks like.

### Step 3: Test the extension play first

Extension is the cheapest play and the most frequently skipped. Before accepting replace or retire,
ask:

1. Is there a **segment** the current product could serve with a variant?
2. Is there a **need** an added capability would meet without re-architecture?
3. Would a **repackage or rebrand** reach a different buyer?
4. Is the decline in the *product*, or in the *channel* or *price* around it?

Question 4 catches a specific and common error: a product judged to be declining when the actual
failure is a distribution channel that stopped working or a bundle that lost its edge. Fixing the
lever is cheaper than replacing the product.

If the honest answer to all four is no, extension is off the table — and now you know why, which
you'll need when someone asks in three months.

### Step 4: If replacing, build the risk register before committing

Walk the seven hazards. For each one that applies, fill all five columns including the contingency.
Rate probability and impact honestly — a register where everything is "low/low" was filled in to be
finished.

Two questions worth forcing:
- **Cannibalization:** which product wins which customer, and what happens to margin during overlap?
- **Hazard 7:** who owns the retirement, and is it funded? A replacement with an unfunded EOL is a
  launch with a liability attached.

### Step 5: If retiring, hand off

The retirement play is a full process of its own. Confirm the two things that most often turn out
to be false — that there's a landing place for customers, and that no contractual or regulatory
obligation blocks the timeline — then move to the EOL suite.

### Step 6: Run it across the line

For a product family, build the portfolio worksheet: every product, its stage, its yes-count, its
pressure source, and its recommended play. Then check the interactions:

- Two products can't both be the replacement for the same customers
- An extension on one product can undercut the case for another's replacement
- Retiring two adjacent products in the same window doubles the customer's disruption, not yours

### Final Step: Offer what comes next

"Where next?

1. **Talk through the diagnosis** — see [`lifecycle-play-advisor`](../lifecycle-play-advisor/SKILL.md)
   if you'd rather be walked through the questions (Recommended)
2. **Run the retirement** — see [`eol-process`](../eol-process/SKILL.md) or
   [`eol-readiness-advisor`](../eol-readiness-advisor/SKILL.md)
3. **Plan the extension** — see [`organic-growth-advisor`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/organic-growth-advisor/SKILL.md) for
   which growth path the variant serves
4. **Build the risk register** for a replacement play in depth

Reply with a number, a combination, or your own path."

---

## Examples

- `examples/sample.md` — Fieldlight product line (SaaS, four modules, three different plays)
- `examples/sample-industrial.md` — Northfield Automation controller line (industrial, a
  replacement play with the risk register that predicted what actually went wrong)

---

## Common Pitfalls

### Pitfall 1: Arguing the Play Before the Diagnosis
**Symptom:** The meeting opens with "should we rebuild it or kill it?"

**Consequence:** The loudest advocate wins, and the product's actual stage never gets established.
Six months later nobody can reconstruct why.

**Fix:** Run the seven transition questions first, in writing. The pattern of yeses usually settles
the argument without anyone having to win it.

---

### Pitfall 2: Skipping Extension Because It's Boring
**Symptom:** The options considered are replace and retire. Extension never comes up.

**Consequence:** You spend a replacement's budget on a product a variant would have carried for
three more profitable years.

**Fix:** Test the four extension questions explicitly and record the answers. "No, because…" is a
useful artifact; silence isn't.

---

### Pitfall 3: Mistaking a Channel Problem for a Product Problem
**Symptom:** Revenue is falling, so the product is judged to be in decline.

**Consequence:** You replace a healthy product while the broken distribution channel or stale
bundle carries straight over to the successor.

**Fix:** Transition question 5 and 6 exist for this. Check the lever before condemning the product.

---

### Pitfall 4: The Register Without a Plan B
**Symptom:** Risks are listed with mitigations. The contingency column is empty or reads "monitor."

**Consequence:** The mitigation fails — they do — and there's no prepared response, so the response
is improvised under time pressure in public.

**Fix:** Every risk rated medium or above gets a real contingency. "What is Plan B?" is the whole
point of the column.

---

### Pitfall 5: Funding the Launch, Not the Retirement
**Symptom:** The replacement play has a GTM budget and no EOL budget.

**Consequence:** Hazard 7. The successor ships, the old product limps on unsupported, and customers
experience the transition as abandonment while you celebrate a launch.

**Fix:** A replacement play is two funded workstreams. If the retirement isn't funded, you have
chosen an extension play with extra steps.

---

## References

### Related Skills

These stand on their own — none is a prerequisite for this skill, and this skill isn't a
prerequisite for them.

- [`lifecycle-play-advisor`](../lifecycle-play-advisor/SKILL.md) — the guided version of this
  diagnosis
- [`eol-readiness-advisor`](../eol-readiness-advisor/SKILL.md) — the retirement play's go/no-go
- [`eol-process`](../eol-process/SKILL.md) — running a retirement end to end
- [`organic-growth-advisor`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/organic-growth-advisor/SKILL.md) — which growth path an extension
  serves
- [`ansoff-matrix`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/ansoff-matrix/SKILL.md) — where the next tranche of growth comes from
- [`roadmap-planning`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/roadmap-planning/SKILL.md) — sequencing the play once it's chosen

### External Frameworks
- Product Life Cycle (PLC) — the five-stage economic model
- Diffusion of innovations / the chasm — why some replacements never cross to the mainstream
- Product Life Cycle strategy grid — marketing-mix levers by stage

### Provenance
- Distilled from practitioner experience running product lifecycle transitions and product
  retirements across software, hardware, and regulated industries.

*Reasons why:* expand into new customer segments · meet diverse customer needs · differentiate from
competitors · boost sales with new variants · strengthen brand loyalty.

*Shape:* the existing product keeps running; you add alongside. Cheapest play, lowest risk, and the
one most often dismissed because it isn't exciting.

**Replacement Play** — introduce a new product to take the place of an existing one, offering
similar or improved capability while phasing the old one out.

*Reasons why:* address supply issues · reduce production costs · eliminate obsolete or unused
features · align with strategic goals · comply with regulatory change.

*Shape:* **GTM and EOL happen simultaneously.** This is the expensive play, and the reason is
structural — see below.

**Retirement Play** — phase the product out without a successor of your own.

*Reasons why:* costs exceed revenue · strategic exit from the market · the core problem stopped
existing · technology made it obsolete.

*Shape:* pure EOL. Customers land somewhere else, possibly a competitor, and the goal becomes
losing the product without losing the customer.

### Why Replacement Is the Expensive Play

On a replacement you are running a **launch and a retirement at the same time, for two products
that compete with each other.** Every GTM risk and every EOL risk applies at once, plus one that
only exists here: cannibalization between your own two products.

Both directions of that failure are instructive:
- **Kodak** feared cannibalizing film and starved its digital business. The fear cost the market.
- **Amgen** cannibalized Epogen with Aranesp deliberately. It worked, and still produced complex
  pricing dynamics they had to manage for years.

Fear it and you lose the future; ignore it and you lose margin. Plan for it and you get a
transition.

### The Seven Replacement Hazards

What goes wrong on a replacement play, with the pattern each one leaves:

| # | Hazard | Pattern |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **GTM process failure** | The successor exists but nobody adopts it (Zune) |
| 2 | **Delayed market entry** | Late launch lets competitors define the category (BlackBerry) |
| 3 | **Internal misalignment** | Siloed R&D, marketing, and sales blunt the launch (New Coke) |
| 4 | **External forces** | Backlash, safety, or macro shocks force withdrawal (Google Glass) |
| 5 | **Regulatory risk** | Compliance missed, or the successor triggers new obligations |
| 6 | **Unexpected cannibalization** | The two products fight each other (Kodak, Amgen) |
| 7 | **Poor EOL management** | The successor lands but the old product's exit is botched (Vista, AT&T POTS, Nest Revolv) |

**Hazard 7 is the one this repo's EOL suite exists to prevent** — and it's the one teams discount
most, because by the time they're planning the launch, the retirement feels like paperwork.

### The Risk Register

For each hazard that applies, fill five columns. The fifth is the one people skip:

| Risk | Probability | Impact | Mitigation | Contingency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| What could adversely affect the business case? | How likely? | How bad? | How do we reduce the probability? | **What is Plan B?** |

A register with no contingency column is a worry list. Plan B is what makes it a plan.

### Anti-Patterns (what this is NOT)
- **Not a growth framework.** Where the next tranche of growth comes from is a different question —
  see `ansoff-matrix` and `organic-growth-advisor`.
- **Not a forecast.** It reasons about stage and direction, not numbers.
- **Not automatic.** Decline is not a death sentence; a mature product throwing off margin with low
  support cost is a harvest, not a project.
- **Not one product at a time, necessarily.** The worksheet runs across a line, and the plays
  interact — two products can't both be the replacement.

---

## Application

Use `template.md` for the worksheet and risk register.

### Step 1: Diagnose the stage

Run the seven transition questions. Count the yeses:

- **0-1 yes** — mature and healthy. The question isn't a play, it's whether to invest more
- **2-3 yes** — mature and softening. Extension play territory; watch quarterly
- **4-5 yes** — crossing into decline. Pick a play deliberately, now
- **6-7 yes** — in decline. Replace or retire; extension likely postpones a decision rather than
  changing an outcome

Write down which questions came back yes. The *pattern* discriminates the plays more than the count
does.

### Step 2: Identify what's driving the pressure

Three sources, and they point at different plays:

| Pressure | Signal | Points toward |
|---|---|---|
| **Demand-side** | Needs shifted, segments moved, competitors differentiated | **Extend** — if the core still solves a real problem for someone |
| **Supply/cost-side** | Components EOL, production cost, support load, strategy shift | **Replace** — the problem is your economics, not the customer's need |
| **Capability-side** | Technology obsolete, architecture at its limit, regulation changed | **Replace** or **Retire** — depends on whether the need survives the technology |

**The trap:** supply-side pressure feels like a customer problem when it reaches the roadmap. "We
need to rebuild this" often means "our costs are bad," which is a legitimate reason for a
replacement — but say it out loud, because it changes what success looks like.

### Step 3: Test the extension play first

Extension is the cheapest play and the most frequently skipped. Before accepting replace or retire,
ask:

1. Is there a **segment** the current product could serve with a variant?
2. Is there a **need** an added capability would meet without re-architecture?
3. Would a **repackage or rebrand** reach a different buyer?
4. Is the decline in the *product*, or in the *channel* or *price* around it?

Question 4 catches a specific and common error: a product judged to be declining when the actual
failure is a distribution channel that stopped working or a bundle that lost its edge. Fixing the
lever is cheaper than replacing the product.

If the honest answer to all four is no, extension is off the table — and now you know why, which
you'll need when someone asks in three months.

### Step 4: If replacing, build the risk register before committing

Walk the seven hazards. For each one that applies, fill all five columns including the contingency.
Rate probability and impact honestly — a register where everything is "low/low" was filled in to be
finished.

Two questions worth forcing:
- **Cannibalization:** which product wins which customer, and what happens to margin during overlap?
- **Hazard 7:** who owns the retirement, and is it funded? A replacement with an unfunded EOL is a
  launch with a liability attached.

### Step 5: If retiring, hand off

The retirement play is a full process of its own. Confirm the two things that most often turn out
to be false — that there's a landing place for customers, and that no contractual or regulatory
obligation blocks the timeline — then move to the EOL suite.

### Step 6: Run it across the line

For a product family, build the portfolio worksheet: every product, its stage, its yes-count, its
pressure source, and its recommended play. Then check the interactions:

- Two products can't both be the replacement for the same customers
- An extension on one product can undercut the case for another's replacement
- Retiring two adjacent products in the same window doubles the customer's disruption, not yours

### Final Step: Offer what comes next

"Where next?

1. **Talk through the diagnosis** — see [`lifecycle-play-advisor`](../lifecycle-play-advisor/SKILL.md)
   if you'd rather be walked through the questions (Recommended)
2. **Run the retirement** — see [`eol-process`](../eol-process/SKILL.md) or
   [`eol-readiness-advisor`](../eol-readiness-advisor/SKILL.md)
3. **Plan the extension** — see [`organic-growth-advisor`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/organic-growth-advisor/SKILL.md) for
   which growth path the variant serves
4. **Build the risk register** for a replacement play in depth

Reply with a number, a combination, or your own path."

---

## Examples

- `examples/sample.md` — Fieldlight product line (SaaS, four modules, three different plays)
- `examples/sample-industrial.md` — Northfield Automation controller line (industrial, a
  replacement play with the risk register that predicted what actually went wrong)

---

## Common Pitfalls

### Pitfall 1: Arguing the Play Before the Diagnosis
**Symptom:** The meeting opens with "should we rebuild it or kill it?"

**Consequence:** The loudest advocate wins, and the product's actual stage never gets established.
Six months later nobody can reconstruct why.

**Fix:** Run the seven transition questions first, in writing. The pattern of yeses usually settles
the argument without anyone having to win it.

---

### Pitfall 2: Skipping Extension Because It's Boring
**Symptom:** The options considered are replace and retire. Extension never comes up.

**Consequence:** You spend a replacement's budget on a product a variant would have carried for
three more profitable years.

**Fix:** Test the four extension questions explicitly and record the answers. "No, because…" is a
useful artifact; silence isn't.

---

### Pitfall 3: Mistaking a Channel Problem for a Product Problem
**Symptom:** Revenue is falling, so the product is judged to be in decline.

**Consequence:** You replace a healthy product while the broken distribution channel or stale
bundle carries straight over to the successor.

**Fix:** Transition question 5 and 6 exist for this. Check the lever before condemning the product.

---

### Pitfall 4: The Register Without a Plan B
**Symptom:** Risks are listed with mitigations. The contingency column is empty or reads "monitor."

**Consequence:** The mitigation fails — they do — and there's no prepared response, so the response
is improvised under time pressure in public.

**Fix:** Every risk rated medium or above gets a real contingency. "What is Plan B?" is the whole
point of the column.

---

### Pitfall 5: Funding the Launch, Not the Retirement
**Symptom:** The replacement play has a GTM budget and no EOL budget.

**Consequence:** Hazard 7. The successor ships, the old product limps on unsupported, and customers
experience the transition as abandonment while you celebrate a launch.

**Fix:** A replacement play is two funded workstreams. If the retirement isn't funded, you have
chosen an extension play with extra steps.

---

## References

### Related Skills

These stand on their own — none is a prerequisite for this skill, and this skill isn't a
prerequisite for them.

- [`lifecycle-play-advisor`](../lifecycle-play-advisor/SKILL.md) — the guided version of this
  diagnosis
- [`eol-readiness-advisor`](../eol-readiness-advisor/SKILL.md) — the retirement play's go/no-go

- [`organic-growth-advisor`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/organic-growth-advisor/SKILL.md) — which growth path an extension
  serves
- [`ansoff-matrix`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/ansoff-matrix/SKILL.md) — where the next tranche of growth comes from
- [`roadmap-planning`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/roadmap-planning/SKILL.md) — sequencing the play once it's chosen

### External Frameworks
- Product Life Cycle (PLC) — the five-stage economic model
- Diffusion of innovations / the chasm — why some replacements never cross to the mainstream
- Product Life Cycle strategy grid — marketing-mix levers by stage

### Provenance
- Distilled from practitioner experience running product lifecycle transitions and product
  retirements across software, hardware, and regulated industries.

# Retention Diagnostic Advisor

## Purpose

Find **why customers leave or go quiet**, and match the fix to the cause. Retention programs fail
when they treat all churn as one problem: a discount saves the customer who found it too expensive
and does nothing for the one who never got started.

The sentence to keep in your head: **churn is the last event, not the cause.** The cause happened
earlier: the customer never got value, was never the right customer, got value and then lost it, or
something around them changed. Each needs a different fix.

## Input

**Works best with:** What's churning or going quiet (which customers, since when) and what you
already know about why.

**Also useful:** Retention or renewal numbers by cohort and segment, exit or cancellation reasons,
time from sign-up to churn, support history of customers who left, and how long a typical contract
runs.

Anything supplied with the invocation itself (text after the skill name, a pasted context dump, or
an appended `ARGUMENTS:` line) counts as answers already given. Use it and skip whatever it covers;
don't re-ask.

**Arriving empty-handed? That works too.** The skill asks what's happening and what you've seen, and
works out which cause is most likely from your answers. If the data can't tell the causes apart, it
says so and names the cheapest way to find out.

**Example invocations:**
- `Churn rose from 6% to 9% last quarter. Most leavers had under 90 days with us.`
- `Service-contract renewals on the NFA-200 base fell from 62% to 48%. Contracts run 3 years.`

---

## Key Concepts

### Four Causes of Leaving

| Cause | What it looks like | Typical timing |
|---|---|---|
| **Never activated** | Customer signed up or bought but never got first value ([`activation-design`](../activation-design/SKILL.md)) | Early: first weeks or months; usage never started |
| **Never a fit** | Wrong customer: wrong size, use case, or expectation set in the sale | Early to mid; leaves after a trial or first renewal |
| **Value faded** | Got value, then stopped: needs changed, usage dropped, a champion left | Mid to late; usage falls before the exit |
| **Something changed** | Budget cut, merger, a competitor, a regulation, a product being retired | Any time; often not about your product |

Most real churn is a mix, but **one usually dominates**. Find it before you act.

### Read the Timeline, Not the Rate

The average churn rate hides the pattern. Look at **when** in the customer's life they leave (by
months since start) and **what they did before** (usage curve, support contacts, champion changes).
Early-life churn points to activation and fit. Churn after a long healthy period points to faded
value or outside change. A usage drop that precedes cancellation by weeks is your earliest warning.

### Segment Before You Conclude

Cut by **customer size, industry, source (direct, partner, self-serve), plan, and the version they
bought**. Retention that is 95% in one segment and 60% in another is two problems, and the weak
segment might be customers you never should have sold to ([`sales-value-narrative`](../sales-value-narrative/SKILL.md)
decides who you tell the story to).

### Stated Reasons Are Weak Evidence

"Too expensive" is the most common exit reason and the least informative: it often means "didn't see
the value." Treat exit reasons as a starting question ("What did you expect it to do for you?"), not
a finding, and compare them with behavior (did they ever activate? did usage fall first?).

### Leading Signals

Watch the signals that move before the exit: **usage trend, breadth of use (how many people or
features), support sentiment, champion turnover, and missed milestones.** For contract businesses
add: engagement with the service, unused entitlements, and who the renewal decision-maker is. A
simple health view built from these is better than waiting for a cancellation. See
[`launch-metrics`](../launch-metrics/SKILL.md) for leading and lagging pairs.

### Who to Save and Who to Let Go

Not every customer is worth saving. Ask: would they have been a good customer if the cause were
fixed? Saving a bad-fit customer at a discount trains the market and fills support with the wrong
requests. Be explicit about the customers you'll try to keep, the ones you'll let go, and why.

### Right-Size the Response

A small contract base needs a conversation with each at-risk account. A large self-serve base needs
an automated health signal and a few targeted plays. Don't build a heavy program to solve a cause the
data hasn't confirmed. Recommend a level and let the user move it.

### Facilitation Source of Truth

Use [`workshop-facilitation`](../workshop-facilitation/SKILL.md) as the interaction protocol:
heads-up, one question per turn, numbered options, and best-guess mode on request.

**Default entry mode:** Guided · set in `pm-skills.config.yaml` (library-wide default or a per-skill override); the user's own choice in the session always wins. On the first turn, offer all three modes, then open in the default without waiting for a pick: Guided asks the first question, Context dump invites the paste, Best guess asks for a one-sentence minimum and drafts with every assumption labeled.

### Anti-Patterns (what this is NOT)
- **Not a retention program.** It diagnoses; the fix depends on the cause.
- **Not a churn forecast.** It explains past behavior and points to early signals.
- **Not a discount strategy.** Price is rarely the cause and is a costly cure.

---

## Application

This skill asks **up to 4 adaptive questions**, then recommends a diagnosis and a move.

### Question 1 of 4: What's happening?

**Agent asks:**

"Describe what you're seeing: who is leaving or going quiet, since when, and what you've noticed
about them."

**Listen for the timeline and the segment.** "Mostly under 90 days" and "mostly large accounts at
renewal" point to different causes.

### Question 2 of 4: When in their life do they leave?

**Agent asks:**

"When do customers typically leave?

1. **Early: before or just after they really start** (first weeks or months)
2. **At the first renewal or trial end**
3. **After a long, healthy period**
4. **No clear pattern / I don't know**"

**Map to the likely cause:** 1 → never activated. 2 → never a fit or never activated. 3 → value
faded or something changed. 4 → say the data can't tell yet and name how to find out.

### Question 3 of 4: Did they ever get started?

**Agent asks:**

"For the customers who left, what do you know about what they did before they left?

1. **Most never really used it** (little or no usage)
2. **They used it, then usage dropped over weeks or months**
3. **They used it until something changed** (a person left, a merger, a budget cut)
4. **I haven't looked at this yet**"

**Confirm or revise.** 1 → activation. 2 → value faded. 3 → something changed. 4 → recommend this
check first; it's the cheapest way to separate the causes.

### Question 4 of 4: Who are they?

**Agent asks:**

"Do the leavers share anything: size, industry, how they came to you, what they bought?"

**Find the segment.** A shared trait suggests a fit problem. No shared trait points to a product or
service cause. Ask how big the base is, so the response can be sized.

### Final Step: Recommend the diagnosis and move

```markdown
## Retention Diagnosis: [context]

**Most likely cause:** [Never activated / Never a fit / Value faded / Something changed],
because [the evidence from their answers]
**Confidence:** [strong / suggestive / thin] · **What would change my mind:** [one check]

### The move
- **If never activated:** [fix the path to first value; see activation-design]
- **If never a fit:** [change who you sell to; adjust the story and qualification]
- **If value faded:** [reinforce value: usage reviews, new use cases, a champion plan]
- **If something changed:** [save plays only where it's winnable; plan for the rest]

### Leading signals to watch
[usage trend, breadth, support sentiment, champion turnover, unused entitlements]

### Who to save and who to let go
[with reasons]

### Next
1. [skill or action]
2. [skill or action]
```

---

## Examples

### Example A: SaaS, early churn

**User:** "Churn rose from 6% to 9% last quarter. Most leavers had under 90 days with us. Leadership
wants a loyalty program."

**Agent (Q2):** → **1 (early).** **(Q3):** → **1 (most never really used it).** **(Q4):** "Mostly
accounts under 100 technicians that came in through the March promo."

**Diagnosis:** *Never activated, with a fit component.* Confidence: suggestive (we have the
timing and the usage, not why). A loyalty program would target customers who never got started. The
move: fix the path to first value ([`activation-design`](../activation-design/SKILL.md)) and look
at who the March promotion brought in. What would change my mind: if the leavers had real usage
before leaving.

### Example B: Industrial, renewals

**User:** "Service-contract renewals on the NFA-200 base fell from 62% to 48%. Contracts run three
years."

**Agent (Q2):** → **2 (at renewal).** **(Q3):** → **3 (something changed):** "Several plants were
told the NFA-200 is being retired." **(Q4):** "Mostly plants with 1-2 units."

**Diagnosis:** *Something changed: the product's end-of-sale announcement.* Confidence: strong
(timing matches the announcement; the leavers share a trait). The move is not a loyalty program but
a clear transition path: contract terms through 2028, a migration offer for the NFA-500, and the
messaging from [`eol-message`](../eol-message/SKILL.md). Save plays for plants with 3+ units; let
the rest migrate on their schedule. What would change my mind: if non-announced plants also drop.

---

## Common Pitfalls

### Pitfall 1: Treating All Churn as One Problem
**Symptom:** One loyalty program for every leaver.
**Consequence:** It misses the cause for most of them.
**Fix:** Separate the four causes first.

### Pitfall 2: Believing the Exit Survey
**Symptom:** "Too expensive" accepted as the cause.
**Consequence:** Discounts that don't save the customer who never got value.
**Fix:** Compare the stated reason with behavior.

### Pitfall 3: Reading the Rate, Not the Timeline
**Symptom:** Tracking the average monthly churn.
**Consequence:** Early-life and late-life problems blur together.
**Fix:** Chart churn by months since start and by segment.

### Pitfall 4: Saving Everyone
**Symptom:** Discounts to every at-risk account.
**Consequence:** Bad-fit customers stay and drain support.
**Fix:** Decide who is worth saving and why.

### Pitfall 5: Waiting for the Cancellation
**Symptom:** Action begins at the cancel request.
**Consequence:** The decision is already made.
**Fix:** Watch leading signals: usage trend, breadth, champion changes.

### Pitfall 6: Ignoring Outside Change
**Symptom:** Churn blamed on the product when a merger or announcement caused it.
**Consequence:** A fix for something that wasn't broken.
**Fix:** Check what changed around the customers.

---

## References

### Related Skills
- [`activation-design`](../activation-design/SKILL.md): fix the path to first value
- [`usage-data-investigation`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/usage-data-investigation/SKILL.md): read usage and cohorts
- [`launch-metrics`](../launch-metrics/SKILL.md): leading and lagging indicators and triggers
- [`saas-revenue-growth-metrics`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/saas-revenue-growth-metrics/SKILL.md): churn and retention definitions
- [`eol-message`](../eol-message/SKILL.md) and [`eol-process`](../eol-process/SKILL.md): when retirement is the cause
- [`organic-growth-advisor`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/organic-growth-advisor/SKILL.md): growth paths beyond retention
- [`workshop-facilitation`](../workshop-facilitation/SKILL.md): interaction protocol

### External Frameworks
- **Cohort retention curves:** standard product and customer analytics practice.
- **Customer health scoring and leading signals:** common customer-success practice.
- **Value realization and time to value:** customer-success literature.

### Provenance
Distilled from practitioner experience diagnosing churn and renewal problems in software and industrial service businesses.

On the first turn, offer all three modes, then open in the default without waiting for a pick: Guided asks the first question, Context dump invites the paste, Best guess asks for a one-sentence minimum and drafts with every assumption labeled.

### Anti-Patterns (what this is NOT)
- **Not a retention program.** It diagnoses; the fix depends on the cause.
- **Not a churn forecast.** It explains past behavior and points to early signals.
- **Not a discount strategy.** Price is rarely the cause and is a costly cure.

---

## Application

This skill asks **up to 4 adaptive questions**, then recommends a diagnosis and a move.

### Question 1 of 4: What's happening?

**Agent asks:**

"Describe what you're seeing: who is leaving or going quiet, since when, and what you've noticed
about them."

**Listen for the timeline and the segment.** "Mostly under 90 days" and "mostly large accounts at
renewal" point to different causes.

### Question 2 of 4: When in their life do they leave?

**Agent asks:**

"When do customers typically leave?

1. **Early: before or just after they really start** (first weeks or months)
2. **At the first renewal or trial end**
3. **After a long, healthy period**
4. **No clear pattern / I don't know**"

**Map to the likely cause:** 1 → never activated. 2 → never a fit or never activated. 3 → value
faded or something changed. 4 → say the data can't tell yet and name how to find out.

### Question 3 of 4: Did they ever get started?

**Agent asks:**

"For the customers who left, what do you know about what they did before they left?

1. **Most never really used it** (little or no usage)
2. **They used it, then usage dropped over weeks or months**
3. **They used it until something changed** (a person left, a merger, a budget cut)
4. **I haven't looked at this yet**"

**Confirm or revise.** 1 → activation. 2 → value faded. 3 → something changed. 4 → recommend this
check first; it's the cheapest way to separate the causes.

### Question 4 of 4: Who are they?

**Agent asks:**

"Do the leavers share anything: size, industry, how they came to you, what they bought?"

**Find the segment.** A shared trait suggests a fit problem. No shared trait points to a product or
service cause. Ask how big the base is, so the response can be sized.

### Final Step: Recommend the diagnosis and move

```markdown
## Retention Diagnosis: [context]

**Most likely cause:** [Never activated / Never a fit / Value faded / Something changed],
because [the evidence from their answers]
**Confidence:** [strong / suggestive / thin] · **What would change my mind:** [one check]

### The move
- **If never activated:** [fix the path to first value; see activation-design]
- **If never a fit:** [change who you sell to; adjust the story and qualification]
- **If value faded:** [reinforce value: usage reviews, new use cases, a champion plan]
- **If something changed:** [save plays only where it's winnable; plan for the rest]

### Leading signals to watch
[usage trend, breadth, support sentiment, champion turnover, unused entitlements]

### Who to save and who to let go
[with reasons]

### Next
1. [skill or action]
2. [skill or action]
```

---

## Examples

### Example A: SaaS, early churn

**User:** "Churn rose from 6% to 9% last quarter. Most leavers had under 90 days with us. Leadership
wants a loyalty program."

**Agent (Q2):** → **1 (early).** **(Q3):** → **1 (most never really used it).** **(Q4):** "Mostly
accounts under 100 technicians that came in through the March promo."

**Diagnosis:** *Never activated, with a fit component.* Confidence: suggestive (we have the
timing and the usage, not why). A loyalty program would target customers who never got started. The
move: fix the path to first value ([`activation-design`](../activation-design/SKILL.md)) and look
at who the March promotion brought in. What would change my mind: if the leavers had real usage
before leaving.

### Example B: Industrial, renewals

**User:** "Service-contract renewals on the NFA-200 base fell from 62% to 48%. Contracts run three
years."

**Agent (Q2):** → **2 (at renewal).** **(Q3):** → **3 (something changed):** "Several plants were
told the NFA-200 is being retired." **(Q4):** "Mostly plants with 1-2 units."

**Diagnosis:** *Something changed: the product's end-of-sale announcement.* Confidence: strong
(timing matches the announcement; the leavers share a trait). The move is not a loyalty program but
a clear transition path: contract terms through 2028, a migration offer for the NFA-500, and the
messaging from [`eol-message`](../eol-message/SKILL.md). Save plays for plants with 3+ units; let
the rest migrate on their schedule. What would change my mind: if non-announced plants also drop.

---

## Common Pitfalls

### Pitfall 1: Treating All Churn as One Problem
**Symptom:** One loyalty program for every leaver.
**Consequence:** It misses the cause for most of them.
**Fix:** Separate the four causes first.

### Pitfall 2: Believing the Exit Survey
**Symptom:** "Too expensive" accepted as the cause.
**Consequence:** Discounts that don't save the customer who never got value.
**Fix:** Compare the stated reason with behavior.

### Pitfall 3: Reading the Rate, Not the Timeline
**Symptom:** Tracking the average monthly churn.
**Consequence:** Early-life and late-life problems blur together.
**Fix:** Chart churn by months since start and by segment.

### Pitfall 4: Saving Everyone
**Symptom:** Discounts to every at-risk account.
**Consequence:** Bad-fit customers stay and drain support.
**Fix:** Decide who is worth saving and why.

### Pitfall 5: Waiting for the Cancellation
**Symptom:** Action begins at the cancel request.
**Consequence:** The decision is already made.
**Fix:** Watch leading signals: usage trend, breadth, champion changes.

### Pitfall 6: Ignoring Outside Change
**Symptom:** Churn blamed on the product when a merger or announcement caused it.
**Consequence:** A fix for something that wasn't broken.
**Fix:** Check what changed around the customers.

---

### Related Skills
- [`activation-design`](../activation-design/SKILL.md): fix the path to first value
- [`usage-data-investigation`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/usage-data-investigation/SKILL.md): read usage and cohorts
- [`launch-metrics`](../launch-metrics/SKILL.md): leading and lagging indicators and triggers
- [`saas-revenue-growth-metrics`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/saas-revenue-growth-metrics/SKILL.md): churn and retention definitions
- [`eol-message`](../eol-message/SKILL.md) and [`eol-process`](../eol-process/SKILL.md): when retirement is the cause
- [`organic-growth-advisor`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/organic-growth-advisor/SKILL.md): growth paths beyond retention
- [`workshop-facilitation`](../workshop-facilitation/SKILL.md): interaction protocol

### External Frameworks
- **Cohort retention curves:** standard product and customer analytics practice.
- **Customer health scoring and leading signals:** common customer-success practice.
- **Value realization and time to value:** customer-success literature.

Distilled from practitioner experience diagnosing churn and renewal problems in software and industrial service businesses.

---

# Sales Value Narrative

## Purpose

Build the story Sales and partners tell: **why change, why now, why us**, then the value for each
person in the buying group, the proof behind each claim, prepared answers to the objections reps
actually hear, and a short **do-not-say** list. The test of a good narrative is whether your
champion can retell it to people you will never meet.

It builds on the [`message-house`](../message-house/SKILL.md) (the pillars become the spine of
"why us") and feeds [`buying-journey-enablement`](../buying-journey-enablement/SKILL.md) (which says
*when* each piece gets used). The one-page competitive card is built by
[`battle-card-builder`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/battle-card-builder/SKILL.md); this skill tells you what the card needs
from the narrative.

## Input

**Works best with:** The offering, who you sell to (the roles in the buying group), and the
alternative you most often lose to, which is often "do nothing."

**Also useful:** The message house, win/loss notes, the objections reps hear (from reps, not from
the product team), proof you hold, and pricing and packaging.

Anything supplied with the invocation itself (text after the skill name, a pasted context dump, or
an appended `ARGUMENTS:` line) counts as answers already given. Use it and skip whatever it covers;
don't re-ask.

**Arriving empty-handed? That works too.** The skill asks who buys and what usually beats you, then
drafts the narrative as labeled hypotheses with every proof point and number left as a
`[NEEDS SOURCE]` blank.

**Example invocations:**
- `Sales narrative for Route Optimizer. We lose to "our dispatchers manage fine in spreadsheets."`
- `Objection handling for the NFA-500: price, switching risk, and "our current supplier is fine."`

---

## Key Concepts

### Narrative, Not Feature Tour

A feature tour starts at your product and leaves the customer to work out why it matters. A
narrative starts at the customer's situation and moves to a better outcome, with your offering as
the way there. In a group purchase the person you're talking to has to sell the decision internally.
Give them a story they can retell.

### Why Change, Why Now, Why Us (in that order)

1. **Why change?** What does the status quo cost? The strongest competitor is usually *doing
   nothing*: the spreadsheet, the old machine, the current supplier. Show the cost of staying put
   in the customer's terms (hours, downtime, errors, risk, compliance).
2. **Why now?** What makes delay expensive? A trigger: a regulation, a renewal date, an aging
   system losing support, rising cost, a new site, an audit. Without a why-now, deals slip to next
   year's budget.
3. **Why us?** What can you do that the alternatives can't, that matters to *this* customer, and
   that they can verify? Differentiation they can't check is a claim, not a reason.

Most sales material starts with "why us," which skips the two questions the customer has to answer
first.

### The Buying Group

Most purchases are decided by a group. Each role weighs different value and fears different risk:

| Role | Typical people | Cares about | Fears |
|---|---|---|---|
| **User** | Dispatchers, operators, technicians | Easier daily work, reliability | More work, being blamed when it fails |
| **Buyer** | Procurement | Price, terms, supplier risk, comparable offers | Overpaying, an unreliable supplier |
| **Technical evaluator** | IT, security, engineering, maintenance | Integration, standards, security, supportability | Integration failure, non-compliance |
| **Finance** | Controller, CFO | Payback, total cost, budget fit | An investment that doesn't pay back, hidden costs |
| **Sponsor** | VP, plant or operations head | The outcome they own | A failed project with their name on it |

Add **gatekeepers** and **influencers** (consultants, integrators) when they matter. In channel
sales the partner is a role too: they need a reason to sell you instead of another brand. Write
value **per role**. If every role gets the same message, it's generic.

### Proof: Sourced or Flagged

A claim without proof is an opinion. Strongest first: independent test or certification; named
reference with written permission; measured result from a pilot or installed base; internal test
with the method available; a calculation the customer can repeat with their own numbers; an
unsupported claim (not proof). Every proof point is sourced or `[NEEDS SOURCE]`. **Never invent
proof**: no made-up customers, quotes, percentages, or awards. A rep who repeats one invented claim
to a technical evaluator loses the deal and the credibility. Comparative claims about a named
competitor carry legal risk; have Legal review them before they leave the building.

### Objection Handling

Objections are information. The structure: **Acknowledge** without arguing; **Clarify** what's
behind it ("too expensive" can mean over budget this year, more than a competitor's quote, or "I
don't believe the savings"); **Respond** with proof matched to the real concern; **Confirm** it
answered. Prepare answers for the objections Sales actually hears, collected from reps, partners,
and win/loss reviews, not the ones the product team would like to answer. Common ones: price,
switching risk, compatibility with what they have, "our current approach is fine," support coverage,
security, and "we'll wait for next budget."

### Trap Questions and the Do-Not-Say List

A **trap question** leads the customer to discover a weakness in the alternative. It's safe only
when you hold the documented answer. Never ask what you can't evidence: a trap built on a guess
hands the competitor the stage. A **do-not-say list** protects reps from claims that are outdated,
unprovable, or invite a counter. Teams skip it most, and it saves the most deals.

### The Narrative and the Battle Card

The narrative stays the same across competitors. What changes per alternative that keeps winning
(each named competitor, plus the status quo) is the traps, the proof, and the do-not-say list, and
that is the **battle card**: one page, thirty seconds, with an as-of date, because competitive facts
go stale. Use [`battle-card-builder`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/battle-card-builder/SKILL.md) to research and draft each
card from public evidence. This skill supplies the story and the objections it rests on.

### Enablement Is Collaboration

The PM brings the value logic, proof, and competitive facts. Sales brings what customers really say
and what works in the room. Partners bring what their people can carry beside a dozen other brands.
Build it with them, test it with two or three reps on real accounts, and revise. A narrative the PM
writes alone and hands over at a launch event is rarely used.

### Facilitation Source of Truth

Use [`workshop-facilitation`](../workshop-facilitation/SKILL.md) as the interaction protocol when
running this conversationally.

**Default entry mode:** Guided · set in `pm-skills.config.yaml` (library-wide default or a per-skill override); the user's own choice in the session always wins. On the first turn, offer all three modes, then open in the default without waiting for a pick: Guided asks the first question, Context dump invites the paste, Best guess asks for a one-sentence minimum and drafts with every assumption labeled.

### Anti-Patterns (what this is NOT)
- **Not a pitch deck.** It is the story and logic a deck should follow.
- **Not messaging architecture.** That is the [`message-house`](../message-house/SKILL.md).
- **Not a battle card.** See [`battle-card-builder`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/battle-card-builder/SKILL.md).
- **Not invented proof.** Every claim is sourced or flagged.

---

## Application

Use [`template.md`](template.md) for the scaffold.

**Output convention.** Artifact first: scope, why change / why now / why us, value by role, proof,
objections, traps, do-not-say, what each competitor card needs. Commentary short, after. Two
stages: a **working draft** where every line carries a provenance tag (`[FROM YOU]`, `[RESEARCH]`,
`[AI-SUGGESTED, VALIDATE THIS]`) and unsupported proof is `[NEEDS SOURCE]`; then a **committed
copy** with tags removed, followed by a ranked **Proof to Gather** list and the **Questions to Ask
Reps** list.

**If the PM brings a deck or narrative, critique first.** Does it open with why us? Is the status
quo named as a competitor? Is there a why-now? Is value written per role? Is every claim sourced,
and every comparison cleared by Legal? Are the objections ones reps actually hear? Is there a
do-not-say list? Name gaps; offer rewrites last.

### Step 1: Confirm Scope
The offering, the roles in the buying group, the sales motion (direct, partner, self-serve with
sales assist), and the alternatives that win, including the status quo.

### Step 2: Cost of the Status Quo
In the customer's terms, with a source or `[NEEDS SOURCE]`. Offer a calculation they can repeat
with their own numbers.

### Step 3: Why Now
Name the trigger events that make delay expensive for this segment, and how a rep spots them.

### Step 4: Why Us, From the Message House
Take the pillars and proof. If no house exists, draft the differentiators and note that other
material may drift from them.

### Step 5: Value by Role
One short block per role: what they care about, the value in their terms, the proof they trust, the
risk to defuse.

### Step 6: Objections, Traps, and Do-Not-Say
Collect real objections from reps. Write acknowledge-clarify-respond-confirm answers. Add trap
questions only where you hold the evidence. Write the do-not-say list.

### Step 7: Hand Off and Hand Back
Note which competitors and status-quo patterns each need a card (point to
[`battle-card-builder`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/battle-card-builder/SKILL.md)), and where each piece is used (point to
[`buying-journey-enablement`](../buying-journey-enablement/SKILL.md)). Close with a short summary
and a numbered ladder, evidence-favored first, labeled `(Recommended)`: test it with two reps on
live deals; gather the missing proof; build a card for the status quo first; or write the partner
version.

---

## Examples

See [`examples/sample.md`](examples/sample.md) (Fieldlight Route Optimizer, SaaS) and
[`examples/sample-industrial.md`](examples/sample-industrial.md) (Northfield NFA-500, hardware).

---

## Common Pitfalls

### Pitfall 1: Starting With Why Us
**Symptom:** The deck opens with company history and features.
**Consequence:** The customer never agrees there is a problem worth solving.
**Fix:** Open with the cost of the status quo, then why now, then why us.

### Pitfall 2: Ignoring "Do Nothing"
**Symptom:** The narrative compares only against named competitors.
**Consequence:** You lose to the spreadsheet or the old machine.
**Fix:** Name the status quo as a competitor and price it.

### Pitfall 3: One Message for Every Role
**Symptom:** The same value statement goes to the user, the buyer, and finance.
**Consequence:** It speaks to none of them.
**Fix:** Write value per role with the proof that role trusts.

### Pitfall 4: Objections From the Product Team
**Symptom:** The objection list is what the product team wishes customers asked.
**Consequence:** Reps meet the real objection with no answer.
**Fix:** Collect from reps, partners, and win/loss.

### Pitfall 5: Traps Built on Guesses
**Symptom:** A rep asks a trap question about a competitor weakness nobody verified.
**Consequence:** The customer or the competitor corrects them, in public.
**Fix:** Ask only what you can evidence.

### Pitfall 6: No Do-Not-Say List
**Symptom:** Reps repeat last year's claims.
**Consequence:** Outdated or unprovable claims reach technical buyers.
**Fix:** Keep a short, dated do-not-say list.

### Pitfall 7: Invented Proof
**Symptom:** AI-drafted narrative with confident percentages and customer names.
**Consequence:** One false claim loses the deal and the credibility.
**Fix:** Sourced or `[NEEDS SOURCE]`. Never invent.

### Pitfall 8: Written Alone, Handed Over at Launch
**Symptom:** The PM writes it and presents it once.
**Consequence:** Nobody uses it.
**Fix:** Build it with reps and partners and test it on live accounts.

---

## References

### Skill Files
- [`template.md`](template.md): narrative, roles, objections, traps, do-not-say
- [`examples/sample.md`](examples/sample.md), [`examples/sample-industrial.md`](examples/sample-industrial.md)

### Related Skills
- [`message-house`](../message-house/SKILL.md): upstream; pillars and proof become "why us"
- [`battle-card-builder`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/battle-card-builder/SKILL.md): builds the one-page card per alternative
- [`competitive-research-snapshot`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/competitive-research-snapshot/SKILL.md): upstream evidence for competitive claims
- [`buying-journey-enablement`](../buying-journey-enablement/SKILL.md): where each piece is used, by whom
- [`positioning-statement`](https://github.com/deanpeters/Product-Manager-Skills/blob/main/skills/positioning-statement/SKILL.md): upstream anchor
- [`launch-plan`](../launch-plan/SKILL.md): the plan's sales readiness rows depend on this
- [`workshop-facilitation`](../workshop-facilitation/SKILL.md): interaction protocol

### External Frameworks
- **Buying group and buying jobs:** common B2B sales research on committee purchasing.
- **Objection handling (acknowledge, clarify, respond, confirm):** standard sales practice with no single originator.

### Provenance
Distilled from practitioner experience enabling sales and partner teams on B2B and industrial offerings.
